topic: The Magic of Averages: Demystifying the Central Limit Theorem
target_audience: University students (Introductory Statistics) or high-level high school students

sections.title: The Hook: Order from Chaos
lecture_lines: Individual events are often unpredictable and chaotic.
But groups of events follow strict, predictable patterns.
This creates order from chaos, forming a bell curve.
animations: Show many yellow (#FFD700) dots ('Space Rabbits') moving randomly left and right across the screen.
A white (#FFFFFF) horizontal axis appears at the bottom; dots begin to stack as they land.
A cyan (#00FFFF) bell curve outline fades in over the accumulated stacks of dots.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Population vs. Sample
lecture_lines: A population represents the entire group we study.
Samples are smaller subsets taken from that population.
Distribution describes the shape and spread of data.
animations: A large orange (#FF8C00) circle labeled 'Population' appears, filled with small [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/cookie.svg] icons.
A green (#00FF00) circle labeled 'Sample' appears as a small group of [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/cookie.svg] icons moves into it.
White (#FFFFFF) labels 'Mean = mu' and 'Mean = x-bar' appear next to the Population and Sample circles respectively.

sections.title: The Experiment: The Sampling Process
lecture_lines: First, we take a random sample of size n.
Next, we calculate the average for that sample.
We repeat this process hundreds or thousands of times.
Each sample mean is plotted on a new graph.
This builds the sampling distribution of the mean.
animations: Highlight a random group of dots from a source to represent 'Sample size n'.
A yellow (#FFFF00) calculation 'Average =...' flashes above the selected dots.
The 'Average' value transforms into a single dot and drops onto a white (#FFFFFF) horizontal axis.
The process repeats rapidly 1000 times, showing many dots dropping.
The dots stack up to form the 'Sampling Distribution' shape.

sections.title: The Core Reveal: The Shape-Shifting Property
lecture_lines: Start with any population shape, even highly skewed ones.
As sample size n increases, something magical happens.
The distribution of sample means begins to shift shape.
It always settles into a symmetrical normal distribution.
This is the core of the Central Limit Theorem.
animations: Display a magenta (#FF00FF) skewed 'Shark Fin' [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/shark.svg] distribution labeled 'Population'.
Show a gray (#AAAAAA) jagged plot of sample means for a small sample size 'n=2'.
The value 'n=30' appears in white (#FFFFFF), and the jagged plot begins to smooth out.
The plot morphs into a symmetrical cyan (#00FFFF) bell curve.
White (#FFFFFF) text 'Central Limit Theorem' and green (#00FF00) 'Normal Distribution' appear as final labels.

sections.title: Mathematical Nuance: Mean and Standard Error
lecture_lines: The sample mean's center matches the original population mean.
As n grows, the bell curve becomes much narrower.
This narrowing is called the standard error.
Formula: standard deviation divided by square root of n.
Larger samples provide much more precise estimates.
animations: Overlay an orange (#FF8C00) population curve and a cyan (#00FFFF) sample mean curve.
A white (#FFFFFF) vertical dashed line appears, aligning the peaks of both curves at 'Mean = mu'.
Animate the cyan curve narrowing and becoming taller as a white 'n' value increases.
The yellow (#FFFF00) formula 'SE = sigma / sqrt(n)' appears next to the narrow curve.
A horizontal arrow indicates the width (Standard Error) shrinking as 'n' grows larger.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Why It Matters
lecture_lines: The CLT is the powerhouse of modern statistics.
We can study any population using normal distribution math.
This allows for accurate predictions from small samples.
animations: Show a khaki (#F0E68C) box representing '1 Million Lightbulbs' [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/light.svg].
Pull out a small cluster of 50 bulbs [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/light.svg] and draw a cyan (#00FFFF) bell curve over them.
A green (#00FF00) arrow labeled 'Inference' points from the small curve back to the large box.
